sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\: \dfrac{2\sin{x}}{3x} .]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\: \dfrac{2\sin{x}}{3x} .]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that as [MATH: x \to 0,] both the numerator and denominator approach [MATH: 0.]

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\: \dfrac{2\sin{x}}{3x} = \dfrac{0}{0},] which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit: [MATH: \displaystyle \lim_{x\to 0}\: \dfrac{\sin{x}}{x} = 1]

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

[MATH: lim_(x → 0)(2\sin x)/(3x)|= lim_(x → 0)((2)/(3) ⋅ (\sin x)/(x)); = (2)/(3) ⋅ lim_(x → 0)(\sin x)/(x); = (2)/(3) ⋅ 1; = (2)/(3)]

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\theta \cot \theta}{4 \cos^2 \theta}.]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate [MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\theta \cot \theta}{4 \cos^2 \theta}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

[MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(θ\cot θ)/(4\cos^{2} θ)|= lim_(θ → 0)((θ)/(4\cos^{2} θ) ⋅ \cot θ); = lim_(θ → 0)((θ)/(4\cos^{2} θ) ⋅ (\cos θ)/(\sin θ)); = lim_(θ → 0)((θ)/(\sin θ) ⋅ (1)/(4\cos θ)); = lim_(θ → 0)(θ)/(\sin θ) ⋅ lim_(θ → 0)(1)/(4\cos θ)]

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

  • Consider the first limit. Notice that as [MATH: \theta \to 0,] both numerator and denominator approach [MATH: 0.]

    So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get [MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{0}{0},] which is an indeterminate form.

    Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following: [MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(θ)/(\sin θ)|= (1)/((lim_(θ → 0)(\sin θ)/(θ))); = (1)/(1); = 1]

  • Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get [MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \:\dfrac{1}{4 \cos \theta} = \dfrac{1}{4\cos 0} = \dfrac14.] Therefore, we have [MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(θ)/(\sin θ) ⋅ lim_(θ → 0)(1)/(4\cos θ)|= 1 ⋅ (1)/(4) = (1)/(4).]

First, we prove the right-sided limit

Content:
On the unit circle, we choose the two points, [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.] The point [MATH: A] lies on the [MATH: x]-axis and the point [MATH: B] is such that the angle [MATH: \theta=\angle AOB] is acute:
[MATH: 0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Content:
Let the point [MATH: C] be the point of intersection of the tangent to this circle at the point [MATH: A] and the line [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{OB}.] The point [MATH: H] is the projection of the point [MATH: B] onto the [MATH: x]-axis. See the illustration below.

Content:
Then, [MATH: OA = OB =1,] [MATH: BH = \sin \theta,] and [MATH: AC = \tan \theta.]

Content:
The area of a triangle [MATH: \triangle OAB] is less than the area of a sector [MATH: OAB], which is less than the area of a triangle [MATH: \triangle OAC\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: {\color{SteelBlue}\mathcal{A}_{\triangle OAB} }\leq {\color{PaleVioletRed}\mathcal{A}_{sec OAB}} \leq { \color{SandyBrown}\mathcal{A}_{\triangle OAC}}.]

Content:
Using the formulas for the area of the triangles and the sector, we get the following:
[MATH: A_{△OAB}|= (1)/(2)OA ⋅ BH; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ \sin θ; = (\sin θ)/(2); A_{sec.OAB}|= πr^{2} ⋅ (θ)/(2π); = π ⋅ 1^{2} ⋅ (θ)/(2π); = (θ)/(2); A_{△OAC}|= (1)/(2)OA ⋅ AC; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ \tan θ; = (\tan θ)/(2)]

Content:
Therefore, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\sin \theta}{2} \leq \dfrac{\theta}{2} \leq \dfrac{\tan \theta}{2}.]

Content:
Multiplying each part of the final inequality by [MATH: \dfrac{2}{\sin \theta},] we obtain
[MATH: 1 \leq \dfrac{\theta}{\sin \theta} \leq \dfrac{1}{\cos{\theta}}.]

Content:
Taking reciprocals and reversing the inequalities yields
[MATH: \cos{\theta} \leq \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} \leq 1.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^+}\cos{\theta} = 1] and [MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^+}1 = 1,]
we get

Content:
[MATH: lim_(θ → 0^{+})\cos θ|≤ lim_(θ → 0^{+})(\sin θ)/(θ) ≤ lim_(θ → 0^{+})1; 1|≤ lim_(θ → 0^{+})(\sin θ)/(θ) ≤ 1,]

Content:
and consequently, the squeeze theorem implies that

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^+} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.]

Content:
Now, we'll use this result to calculate [MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^-} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta}.]

Content:
Let [MATH: u=-\theta.] Then, the limit [MATH: \theta \to 0^-] is equivalent to [MATH: u \to 0^+.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(θ → 0^{−})(\sin θ)/(θ)|= lim_(u → 0^{+})(\sin (− u))/((− u)); = lim_(u → 0^{+})(− \sin u)/(− u); = lim_(u → 0^{+})(\sin u)/(u); = 1.]

Content:
Finally, since
[MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0^+} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = \lim_{\theta \to 0^-} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta}=1,]
we conclude that
[MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.]

Let's now evaluate the limits separately:

- Consider the first limit. Notice that as [MATH: \theta \to 0,] both numerator and denominator approach [MATH: 0.]

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get
[MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0}\: \dfrac{\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{0}{0},]
which is an indeterminate form.

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:
[MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(θ)/(\sin θ)|= (1)/((lim_(θ → 0)(\sin θ)/(θ))); = (1)/(1); = 1]
- Consider the second limit. Evaluating it directly, we get
[MATH: \lim_\limits{\theta \to 0} \:\dfrac{1}{4 \cos \theta} = \dfrac{1}{4\cos 0} = \dfrac14.]
Therefore, we have
[MATH: lim_(θ → 0)(θ)/(\sin θ) ⋅ lim_(θ → 0)(1)/(4\cos θ)|= 1 ⋅ (1)/(4) = (1)/(4).]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Proof of the Result

Content:
Now, we will prove the limit

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta}=1.]

Content:
First, we prove the right-sided limit
[MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0^+} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta}=1.]

Content:
On the unit circle, we choose the two points, [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.] The point [MATH: A] lies on the [MATH: x]-axis and the point [MATH: B] is such that the angle [MATH: \theta=\angle AOB] is acute:
[MATH: 0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}]

Content:
Let the point [MATH: C] be the point of intersection of the tangent to this circle at the point [MATH: A] and the line [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{OB}.] The point [MATH: H] is the projection of the point [MATH: B] onto the [MATH: x]-axis. See the illustration below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/be6e7265341e98f4865886c48524c3b1]

Content:
Then, [MATH: OA = OB =1,] [MATH: BH = \sin \theta,] and [MATH: AC = \tan \theta.]

Content:
The area of a triangle [MATH: \triangle OAB] is less than the area of a sector [MATH: OAB], which is less than the area of a triangle [MATH: \triangle OAC\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: {\color{SteelBlue}\mathcal{A}_{\triangle OAB} }\leq {\color{PaleVioletRed}\mathcal{A}_{sec OAB}} \leq { \color{SandyBrown}\mathcal{A}_{\triangle OAC}}.]

Content:
Using the formulas for the area of the triangles and the sector, we get the following:
[MATH: A_{△OAB}|= (1)/(2)OA ⋅ BH; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ \sin θ; = (\sin θ)/(2); A_{sec.OAB}|= πr^{2} ⋅ (θ)/(2π); = π ⋅ 1^{2} ⋅ (θ)/(2π); = (θ)/(2); A_{△OAC}|= (1)/(2)OA ⋅ AC; = (1)/(2) ⋅ 1 ⋅ \tan θ; = (\tan θ)/(2)]

Content:
Therefore, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\sin \theta}{2} \leq \dfrac{\theta}{2} \leq \dfrac{\tan \theta}{2}.]

Content:
Multiplying each part of the final inequality by [MATH: \dfrac{2}{\sin \theta},] we obtain
[MATH: 1 \leq \dfrac{\theta}{\sin \theta} \leq \dfrac{1}{\cos{\theta}}.]

Content:
Taking reciprocals and reversing the inequalities yields
[MATH: \cos{\theta} \leq \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} \leq 1.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^+}\cos{\theta} = 1] and [MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^+}1 = 1,]
we get

Content:
[MATH: lim_(θ → 0^{+})\cos θ|≤ lim_(θ → 0^{+})(\sin θ)/(θ) ≤ lim_(θ → 0^{+})1; 1|≤ lim_(θ → 0^{+})(\sin θ)/(θ) ≤ 1,]

Content:
and consequently, the squeeze theorem implies that

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^+} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.]

Content:
Now, we'll use this result to calculate [MATH: \lim\limits_{\theta \to 0^-} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta}.]

Content:
Let [MATH: u=-\theta.] Then, the limit [MATH: \theta \to 0^-] is equivalent to [MATH: u \to 0^+.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: lim_(θ → 0^{−})(\sin θ)/(θ)|= lim_(u → 0^{+})(\sin (− u))/((− u)); = lim_(u → 0^{+})(− \sin u)/(− u); = lim_(u → 0^{+})(\sin u)/(u); = 1.]

Content:
Finally, since
[MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0^+} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = \lim_{\theta \to 0^-} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta}=1,]
we conclude that
[MATH: \lim_{\theta \to 0} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\theta} = 1.]
